title: Vote 2026: President Trump returns to North Carolina as early voting turnout surges statewide in midterm elections - ABC11 News

Vote 2026: President Trump returns to North Carolina as early voting turnout surges statewide in midterm elections - ABC11 Raleigh-Durham 
 24/7 Live Raleigh Durham Fayetteville Surrounding Area POLITICS 
 Vote 2026: President Trump returns to North Carolina as early voting turnout surges 
 President Donald Trump rallied support for GOP candidates at Pitt-Greenville Airport. By Tom George Wednesday, October 21, 2026 3:18AM Share GREENVILLE, N.C. (WTVD) -- President Donald Trump held a rally in eastern North Carolina on Tuesday evening as he worked to drum up support for Republican candidates ahead of the November midterms.
 This is his second visit to the Tar Heel state within the last month.
 The visit came as North Carolina voters are heading to the early voting polls at a pace well ahead of the 2022 midterm election, as national political figures descend on the state, and campaigns intensify their efforts to drive turnout.
 Through Sunday, 525,970 ballots had been cast statewide, up more than 37% from the same point in the 2022 midterms.
 "These numbers are really set to break some records," said Dr. Michael Bitzer, a political science professor at Catawba College.
 Tuesday's rally came after Republicans shifted some funding away from North Carolina to focus on other states. ABC11 asked Jason Simmons, the chairman of the NC GOP, about the war in Iran, which has seen wide disapproval
 Simmons said that despite the polling, he is defending the president.
 "For 50 years, Iran has been a threat and destructive force taking the lives of many in the region, including our men and women in service, and so what you're seeing from the president is a short-term pain for a generational gain," Simmons said.
 The NCGOP acknowledged the recent polls spelling trouble, but it also said that this rally is more about getting out the core base of support
 Trump spoke for more than 90 minutes and told the crowd that Michael Whatley was his choice from the start to run for Senate.
 "You know, I'm the one who said, Michael, I want you to run for Senate. I'm the one who got him into this ... I hope it works," Trump said with a chuckle.
 Trump said that even though it's not his name on the ticket, a vote for Whatley is a vote for his policies.
 "Pretend I'm on the ballot because in a way, I am on the ballot because they want to do away with all of the tremendous things we've done -- the tax cuts, the border," Trump said.
 The president also brought out Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick to announce a new investment in North Carolina by Sibelco to support semiconductor manufacturing.
 "It's quartz manufacturing. Basically, the foundation of semiconductors, and they're going to build it right here in North Carolina," Lutnick said. "Hundreds of millions of dollars."
 Trump led an event in Gastonia in September where he spoke exclusively with ABC11. 
 North Carolina has several high-profile races up and down the ballot, including for US Senate, where former NCGOP and RNC Chairman Whatley faces off against former Gov. Roy Cooper. Sen. Thom Tillis, who holds the seat, announced last year his plans to retire .
 Cooper's campaign responded on Tuesday night to Trump's North Carolina appearance.
 "Independent fact-checkers have called these attacks false - Michael Whatley is getting desperate, and it's shameful that he's using heinous crimes to try to deceive North Carolinians," a Cooper campaign spokesperson told ABC11. "While Roy spent his career putting rapists and violent criminals behind bars and signing tough-on-crime laws as governor, Michael Whatley has continued to knowingly appoint, campaign with, and elevate convicted child sex predators who spent time in prison and is celebrating the support of a president who released over 13,000 prisoners during COVID without a court order."
 Michael Whatley, speaking alongside Trump, contrasted his campaign with Democratic rival Cooper rather than heaping praise on Trump.
 Whatley attacked Cooper, a former two-term governor, over his handling of crime.
 "Who is Roy Cooper going to stand with? Who is he going to fight for?" Whatley said.
 Cook Political Report has listed two US House Seats -- District 1 and District 11 -- as "toss-ups," expected to be the most competitive in North Carolina this cycle.
 District 1 will feature a rematch of 2024 between incumbent Congressman Don Davis, a Democrat, and Republican challenger Laurie Buckhout. The Republican-controlled General Assembly redrew district lines last year, as is within its purview, to make it more favorable to Republicans.
 In District 11, State House Rep. Jennifer Balkcom is facing off against Democrat Jamie Ager, a farmer. The seat is held by Republican Congressman Chuck Edwards, who announced in August he would not seek re-election following a House ethics investigation into his conduct.
 Trump brought up Buckhout and Balkcom to the stage, who he said were expected to have "close races."
 "We have to get them in. We have to vote for them," Trump told the crowd.
 Trump said House Speaker Mike Johnson asked him to give the two "a special callout tonight because they're going to have close races."
 Trump also called up the same two candidates to the stage when he campaigned in the state last month.
 The rally ended after the president headlined the event for just under two hours.
 Trump said he planned to come back to the hotly contested state ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms.
 A series of protesters disrupted Trump's rally in Greenville. The fifth one said: "Gas is too expensive."
 Rally attendees frequently shouted "USA, USA" during the interruptions.
 Trump largely focused on crime during his rally speech rather than the economy.
 Greenville is in Pitt County, part of the state's 3rd Congressional District. However, it borders several counties in the 1st District, presenting a key opportunity for Buckhout to connect with voters.
 - The Associated Press contributed.
